{{Short description|Theorem of quantum information processing}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
In [[physics]], the '''no-broadcasting theorem''' is a result of [[Quantum information science|quantum information theory]].  In the case of [[Pure state|pure quantum states]], it is a [[Theorem|corollary]] of the [[no-cloning theorem]]. The no-cloning theorem for pure states says that it is impossible to create two copies of an unknown state given a single copy of the state. Since [[quantum state]]s cannot be copied in general, they cannot be broadcast.  Here, the word "broadcast" is used in the sense of conveying the state to two or more recipients.  For multiple recipients to each receive the state, there must be, in some sense, a way of duplicating the state.  The no-broadcast theorem generalizes the no-cloning theorem for [[Mixed state (physics)|mixed states]].

The theorem<ref name="nobroadcasting2">{{cite journal|last1=Barnum|first1=Howard|last2=Caves|first2=Carlton M.|author-link2=Carlton M. Caves|last3=Fuchs|first3=Christopher A. |author-link3=Christopher A. Fuchs |last4=Jozsa|first4=Richard|author-link4=Richard Jozsa|last5=Schumacher|first5=Benjamin|author-link5=Benjamin Schumacher|date=1996-04-08|title=Noncommuting Mixed States Cannot Be Broadcast|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=76|issue=15|pages=2818–2821|arxiv=quant-ph/9511010|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.76.2818|pmid=10060796 |bibcode=1996PhRvL..76.2818B |s2cid=11724387 |issn=0031-9007}}</ref> also includes a converse: if two quantum states do [[Commutative property|commute]], there is a method for broadcasting them: they must have a common basis of eigenstates [[diagonalizing]] them simultaneously, and the map that clones every state of this basis is a legitimate quantum operation, requiring only physical resources independent of the input state to implement—a [[completely positive map]].  A corollary is that there is a physical process capable of broadcasting every state in some set of quantum states if, and only if, every pair of states in the set commutes. This broadcasting map, which works in the commuting case, produces an overall state in which the two copies are perfectly correlated in their [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenbasis]].

Remarkably, the theorem does not hold if more than one copy of the initial state is provided: for example, broadcasting six copies starting from four copies of the original state is allowed, even if the states are drawn from a non-commuting set.  The purity of the state can even be increased in the process, a phenomenon known as [[superbroadcasting]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=D'Ariano|first1=Giacomo Mauro|author-link=Giacomo Mauro D'Ariano|last2=Macchiavello|first2=Chiara|last3=Perinotti|first3=Paolo|date=2005-08-05|title=Superbroadcasting of Mixed States|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=95|issue=6|article-number=060503|arxiv=quant-ph/0506251|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.95.060503|pmid=16090933 |bibcode=2005PhRvL..95f0503D |s2cid=2978617 |issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

== Generalized no-broadcast theorem ==
The generalized quantum no-broadcasting theorem, originally proven by Barnum, [[Carlton M. Caves|Caves]], [[Christopher A. Fuchs|Fuchs]], [[Richard Jozsa|Jozsa]] and [[Benjamin Schumacher|Schumacher]] for mixed states of finite-dimensional quantum systems,<ref name="nobroadcasting2" /> says that given a pair of quantum states which do not commute, there is no method capable of taking a single copy of either state and succeeding, no matter which state was supplied and without incorporating knowledge of which state has been supplied, in producing a state such that one part of it is the same as the original state and the other part is also the same as the original state.  That is, given an initial unknown [[Mixed quantum state|state]] <math>\rho_i,</math> drawn from the set <math> \{\rho_i\}_{i \in \{1,2\}}</math> such that <math>[\rho_1,\rho_2] \ne 0</math>, there is no process (using physical means independent of those used to select the state) guaranteed to create a state <math>\rho_{AB}</math> in a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H_A \otimes H_B</math> whose [[partial trace]]s are <math>\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB} = \rho_i</math> and <math>\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB} = \rho_i</math>.  Such a process was termed broadcasting in that paper.

== No-local-broadcasting theorem ==
The second theorem states that local broadcasting is only possible when the state is a classical probability distribution.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|title=On Quantum No-Broadcasting|url=https://link.springer.com/epdf/10.1007/s11005-010-0389-1?sharing_token=iszqKKtl5PQn3Z3o0zzRLPe4RwlQNchNByi7wbcMAY53B3x3PD8d78OwZ1RAR8IktfDHbO4kZZAlLYQo0rTfpOREIlcwn70lG7uJgloU3FZCk1WuqJypS1OeKfwtC4qZSy829VxKRMTbGa5-bBMKpu0QHf2tdNsCMlZGO7K1I60%3D|access-date=2020-10-16|journal=Letters in Mathematical Physics| year=2010 | doi=10.1007/s11005-010-0389-1 | last1=Luo | first1=Shunlong | volume=92 | issue=2 | pages=143–153 | bibcode=2010LMaPh..92..143L | s2cid=121819242 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> This means that a state can only be broadcast locally if it does not have any quantum correlations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Piani|first1=Marco|last2=Horodecki|first2=Pawel|last3=Horodecki|first3=Ryszard|date=2008-03-06|title=No-local-broadcasting theorem for quantum correlations|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=100|issue=9|article-number=090502|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.090502|pmid=18352686 |issn=0031-9007|arxiv=0707.0848|s2cid=42381925 }}</ref> Luo reconciled this theorem with the generalized no-broadcast theorem by making the conjecture that when a state is a classical-quantum state, correlations (rather than the state itself) in a [[Bipartite graph|bipartite]] state can be locally broadcast.<ref name=":3" /> By mathematically proving that his conjecture and the two theorems all relate to and imply one another, Luo proved that all three statements are logically equivalent.<ref name=":3" />
